title: Steering Vectors as a Training Signal in LLM Post-Training
content:
Computer Science > Machine Learning

Title:Steering Vectors as a Training Signal in LLM Post-Training
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Steering vectors (SVs) are residual-stream directions that shift the behavior of LLMs when added to hidden states at inference time. While prior work has mainly used SVs as post-hoc controls, we ask whether the same directions can also guide parameter updates during post-training. We study this question across supervised learning, including SFT and distillation, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Our framework considers two intervention regimes: a hidden-state hook during teacher-forced supervised training, and an advantage-repair mechanism on wrong rollouts in GRPO. For each regime, we analyze three design axes, which are the steering direction, its placement, and the operation used to combine it with training. In supervised settings, SV injection improves over plain SFT and distillation, with gains scaling with the off-policy gap and reaching up to a $12\%$ improvement when distilling from thinking-mode teachers. These gains hold across three random seeds. In RL settings, applying a correctness-contrast direction as advantage repair on wrong rollouts, including otherwise zero-gradient all-wrong groups, recovers a learning signal that transfers to held-out math benchmarks and acts as a composable auxiliary signal that adds to existing zero-variance remedies such as entropy-aware advantage shaping. We further identify three failure boundaries. In detail, code generation can break the direction, cross-family layer transfer can break the placement, and inference-time application on an SV-trained checkpoint can break the intervention regime. Together, these results establish steering vectors as a conditional but effective training signal for LLM post-training. Our code is available here.

report.summary: New research shows steering vectors can do more than control LLM behavior at inference—they can guide post-training, improving SFT, distillation, and RLVR under specific conditions.
report.background: Steering vectors are residual-stream directions that, when added to hidden states at inference time, shift model behavior such as tone, refusal, or reasoning style. Prior work has mostly treated them as post-hoc controls: train a model, then steer it. But post-training itself faces hard problems. Supervised fine-tuning and distillation can suffer from off-policy gaps, especially when distilling from strong thinking-mode teachers. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, such as GRPO, often receives sparse signals and can stall when all rollouts in a group are wrong, producing zero gradient. This paper asks whether the same behavioral directions can also act as a training signal—guiding parameter updates rather than only inference-time behavior—across supervised learning and RLVR.
key_points: The paper studies two intervention regimes: a hidden-state hook during teacher-forced supervised training for SFT and distillation, and an advantage-repair mechanism on wrong rollouts in GRPO. It analyzes three design axes: the steering direction, where it is placed, and how it is combined with training.

In supervised settings, injecting steering vectors improves over plain SFT and distillation. Gains scale with the off-policy gap and reach up to 12% improvement when distilling from thinking-mode teachers. The results hold across three random seeds.

In RL settings, applying a correctness-contrast direction as advantage repair on wrong rollouts recovers a learning signal, including in otherwise zero-gradient all-wrong groups. The signal transfers to held-out math benchmarks and composes with existing zero-variance remedies such as entropy-aware advantage shaping.

The authors identify three failure boundaries: code generation can break the steering direction, cross-family layer transfer can break the placement, and applying inference-time steering to an SV-trained checkpoint can break the intervention regime.

Overall, steering vectors are presented as a conditional but effective training signal, not a universal plug-in. Their value depends on task domain, model family, layer choice, and whether the intervention matches training versus inference.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this expands steering vectors from inference-time control into post-training tooling. It suggests cheaper ways to improve distillation from strong teachers and to rescue sparse-reward RL runs, especially all-wrong rollout groups. For developers, it opens a design space around direction selection, layer placement, and combination operations, but the failure boundaries mean it is not plug-and-play: code generation, cross-family transfer, and inference-time reuse require care. For regular users, the near-term effect is likely indirect—better math reasoning and more reliable fine-tuned models—rather than a visible new feature. The broader lesson is that activation-level signals can serve as auxiliary training objectives, not just deployment controls.
report.tools: Watch the paper’s linked code release on arXiv or GitHub. For steering-vector experimentation, explore TransformerLens, nnsight, repeng, and activation-steering libraries. For post-training and GRPO/RLVR workflows, follow TRL, verl, and OpenRLHF. These tools let developers reproduce SV injection, advantage repair, and distillation experiments.
